title: Design a Community Notification Platform
prompt:
Design notifications for an online community. Events such as replies, mentions, moderation actions, and new activity may create user-visible inbox items and optional mobile push notifications. Users can mute communities or threads, set quiet hours, manage devices, and mark notifications read. The product should aggregate noisy activity without losing important moderation events.

Cover:

- Durable event ingestion and the split between an inbox record and delivery to an external push provider.
- Aggregation, mutes, quiet hours, and a final eligibility gate just before delivery.
- Read state, real-time inbox updates, device attempts, retries, and duplicate handling.
- High-fanout events, provider failures, privacy, observability, and the difference between exactly-once state changes and at-least-once pushes.

Make the delivery and freshness contract explicit before drawing queues.

response.placeholder: Separate durable inbox materialization from best-effort external delivery. Then define aggregation keys, policy checks at creation and send time, read state, device attempt records, and the duplicate boundary.
response.reference_answer:
## 1. Assumptions and notification contract

I would separate a durable inbox promise from a best-effort push promise. A source event is accepted after it is durable and has a stable event ID. A recipient's inbox item is durable only after the notification materializer has written it; a push is an attempt to alert about that item and may be delayed, suppressed, or delivered more than once by external infrastructure. Moderation and safety notices use a higher-priority policy that is not merged into ordinary social activity.

The authoritative data includes user identity, membership and visibility rules, notification preferences, mutes, quiet-hour schedule, devices, inbox items, read state, and policy version. Push payloads are minimized: the device should fetch the inbox item after authentication rather than receive sensitive content as an uncontrolled source of truth.

## 2. Inbox materialization and aggregation

An event gateway writes a validated immutable event and an outbox record in one transaction. Fanout workers use the event ID as an idempotency key, resolve eligible recipients, and write an inbox item or atomically update an aggregation bucket. A bucket key can include recipient, notification class, community or thread, and a short time interval. Its durable state stores aggregate count, selected actors, latest event time, priority, and the event IDs already applied through a bounded deduplication strategy.

Initial materialization consults membership and mute policy to avoid unnecessary writes. It still records the policy version used, because preferences can change after the inbox item exists. Read state is a recipient-owned transition such as unread, seen, or read; it is not inferred from whether a push provider accepted a request. A paginated inbox reads materialized rows and can return a cursor tied to a recipient-local inbox generation.

## 3. Delivery hot path and real-time updates

A delivery scheduler selects due unread inbox items. Immediately before a push attempt, it performs a final eligibility gate against current account status, mutes, quiet hours, device consent, and notification priority. Quiet hours may defer ordinary activity to a scheduled summary while allowing urgent policy notices through. This final check prevents a stale queue from sending a notification after a user muted the thread.

For each eligible device, create a durable attempt record keyed by `(notification_id, device_id, channel, attempt_number)` and lease it to a worker. The worker calls the provider with a stable collapse or message key, records the provider response, and retries only transient failures with bounded backoff. The inbox write also publishes a recipient-scoped event to the real-time service; authenticated clients receive it through SSE or a websocket and reconcile from the inbox API after reconnect.

## 4. Failures, privacy, and observability

A provider timeout creates an ambiguous result: retrying can produce a duplicate device alert, so the system aims for at-least-once push with collapse keys, not an impossible exactly-once guarantee. In contrast, inbox materialization, aggregation updates, and read-state transitions can be idempotent database state changes. Device-token invalidation, account deletion, and mute changes revoke or suppress future attempts and trigger asynchronous cleanup.

For large audiences, fan out in partitioned recipient batches with priority lanes and backpressure. A high-volume thread should aggregate before it expands into millions of individual delivery jobs. Data access is recipient scoped; encrypted device tokens, redacted logs, retention rules, and authorization checks protect activity metadata. Monitor source-to-inbox lag, aggregation ratio, policy and quiet-hour suppression reasons, unread depth, realtime reconnect recovery, delivery attempt outcomes, retry age, provider latency, token invalidations, and read conversion by class.

## 5. Trade-offs

Materializing inbox rows makes reads, read state, and reconnect recovery simple, but costs storage for high fanout. Fanout-on-read saves writes but makes unread counts and real-time delivery hard and spreads policy work across every read. Aggregation lowers notification fatigue and delivery cost, but needs a product-controlled window and exceptions for urgent classes.

Checking policy both while materializing and immediately before sending costs an extra lookup, yet protects users when a preference changes after work entered a queue. Provider collapse keys reduce duplicate annoyance but do not prove a device displayed one alert; the durable inbox remains the user-visible truth.

## Progressive Hints

1. An inbox item and a push notification have different durability and retry semantics.
2. Aggregate social events before creating a per-device delivery job.
3. A mute can be created after an inbox item was queued, so check it again before sending.
4. Treat read state as user data, not as a provider callback.
5. Use a stable notification ID to make inbox updates idempotent, but expect external push delivery to be at least once.
